This relatively protracted nestling period allows for the full development of flight feathers and the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves to meet the energetic demands of post-fledging dispersal. The timing of fledging is tightly coupled with local food availability, as chicks must attain a critical body condition before venturing from the nest. Parental ibises continue to provide supplemental feedings for a short period after fledging, gradually transitioning the young to independent foraging. This gradual weaning process reduces post-fledging mortality and facilitates the acquisition of essential foraging skills, such as probing mudflats for aquatic invertebrates.

This disparity in adult body mass likely arises from differential selective pressures on the sexes, with larger males potentially benefiting from enhanced competitive ability during territorial disputes over nesting sites. Females, by contrast, may face energetic constraints associated with egg production and incubation, which could limit the resources available for somatic growth. These sex-specific mass values were derived from field measurements of breeding adults at colonies in eastern Australia, providing a robust empirical baseline for intraspecific comparisons.

The first successful breeding attempt, however, typically occurs considerably later in life, as individuals must first secure a suitable nesting territory and acquire sufficient body condition.
